title: 3-Read Friday #107: AI Literacy Day Special Edition
author: Craig Barton
summary: For AI Literacy Day, 3-Read Friday #107 breaks from its usual format: Barton hands two of the three picks to Eedi colleagues. Chief Impact Officer Bibi selects a benchmark study by Maxime Lelievre and colleagues testing whether large language models actually possess pedagogical knowledge -- spotting misconceptions, choosing instructional strategies, applying learning theory -- finding that general language ability does not guarantee teaching effectiveness. Chief Data Scientist Simon selects a piece by Kiryn Hoffman, Erin Mote, and Lynne Parker arguing for AI literacy education for children, moving past polarised risk-versus-opportunity framing toward concrete, accessible AI-literacy interventions. Barton's own pick highlights a free, teacher-made Year 7 maths 'Do Now' app for spaced retrieval by Mr Salisbury, which he frames as an example of the democratisation of resource creation that AI now enables. Together the three picks span the research, policy, and grassroots-practice angles on AI literacy in schools.
points: The Lelievre et al. pedagogical-knowledge benchmark tests LLMs on real teaching tasks -- spotting misconceptions, choosing instructional strategies, applying learning theory -- and finds general language fluency does not guarantee teaching effectiveness.

Hoffman, Mote, and Parker push past the standard polarised AI-risk framing toward concrete, already-accessible AI-literacy interventions for kids, which Barton flags as the genuinely useful part of the piece.
Barton's own pick (Mr Salisbury's free Year 7 spaced-retrieval Do Now app) exemplifies a trend he has praised elsewhere: teachers using AI to build and share bespoke classroom resources themselves.
The special guest-picks format itself is notable: Barton deliberately ceded two of three selections to colleagues for AI Literacy Day, broadening the newsletter's usual single-editorial-voice format.
quotes: I chose this because most AI literacy conversations focus on how to use the tools; the harder question is whether AI actually knows how to teach.

This benchmark tests leading models on real pedagogical tasks: spotting misconceptions, choosing instructional strategies, applying learning theory. The finding that general language ability doesn't guarantee teaching effectiveness matters for every educator evaluating AI in their classroom.
At the Stanford AI+Education Summit, there was a lot of discussion about the risks of AI, but not many practical next steps.

The article starts with the standard polarised society framing, which is a great summary if you are not familiar, but the good bit is towards the end, concrete examples of AI literacy solutions you can access now.

Teachers are increasingly feeling empowered by AI to create bespoke resources for their classes. Here is another example, from Mr Salisbury, who has created -- and shared! -- a resource for building spaced retrieval opportunities into his Do Now.
